title: URL Shortener Scaling
description: Scale a URL shortener to billions of redirects: sharding by hash prefix, read replicas for sub-10ms redirects, Kafka-based analytics pipelines, and geographic DNS routing.

segments.text: Bitly processes over ten billion redirects per month. That's roughly four thousand redirects per second sustained, with spikes to fifty thousand during viral content. The read-to-write ratio is extreme — a thousand reads for every write. This ratio drives every architectural decision.

Shard your URL database by hash prefix. Take the first two characters of the short code — that gives you thirty-six squared, about thirteen hundred possible shards. Each shard holds a range of short codes. Lookups are O(1) — hash the short code, find the shard, query directly. No scatter-gather needed.

Redirect latency directly affects user experience. Every millisecond matters — users are waiting for their destination page. Use read replicas aggressively. Three read replicas per shard, with the URL mapping cached in Redis. Cache hit ratio should be above ninety-nine percent since popular links are accessed thousands of times.

Analytics is the money-making feature. Every click generates an event: timestamp, referrer, country, device, browser. Writing this synchronously would destroy redirect latency. Instead, fire-and-forget to Kafka. A Flink pipeline aggregates clicks into hourly, daily, and monthly rollups. Real-time dashboards read from the aggregated data.

A viral tweet includes your short URL. Traffic spikes from four thousand to two hundred thousand redirects per second in thirty seconds. Your cache is warm for this URL but your analytics pipeline is backing up. What do you do?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you handle a 50x traffic spike without degrading redirect latency or losing analytics data?

segments.text: Geographic DNS routing puts redirect servers close to users. Route53 or Cloudflare DNS resolves your short domain to the nearest data center. A user in Tokyo hits the Tokyo redirect server, not one in Virginia. This alone can shave fifty to one hundred and fifty milliseconds off redirect latency by eliminating cross-ocean round trips.

Cache hierarchy matters. L1 cache: in-process LRU for the hottest thousand URLs — sub-microsecond lookups. L2 cache: Redis cluster with the top million URLs — sub-millisecond. L3: database with read replicas — single-digit milliseconds. Most redirects never hit the database. Bitly's cache hit ratio exceeds ninety-nine point five percent.

Hot link handling is a special case. When a URL goes viral, one cache key gets hammered. Use local caching to absorb the load — each server caches the hot URL locally, eliminating Redis round trips entirely. Detect hot keys by tracking access frequency and promoting them to L1 automatically.

HTTP 301 permanent redirect versus 302 temporary — this affects both caching and analytics. 301 tells browsers to cache the redirect forever. Great for performance, terrible for analytics — you stop seeing clicks. 302 forces the browser to hit your server every time. Most URL shorteners use 302 or 307 to preserve analytics visibility.
You need to design a URL shortener that handles one hundred million daily redirects across three continents with sub-ten-millisecond p99 latency. Walk through your complete architecture.
segments.thought_prompt: Design a geo-distributed URL shortener for 100M daily redirects with sub-10ms p99 latency.

segments.text: Scaling a URL shortener is a masterclass in read-heavy system design. Shard by hash prefix for write distribution, layer caches aggressively for read performance, use Kafka for async analytics, and deploy globally with geographic DNS. The read-to-write ratio means optimizing reads is where you spend ninety-nine percent of your engineering effort.
